q: 'Pfah!' said Naphur, crossing his hairy arms. 'I don't know what makes you two believe you deserve such input. Especially you, young man!'
2011, Sam Bowring, Prophecy's Ruin, page 164:
'I should care. Pfah!' said my father, meaning that he shouldn't care and that was the least of his worries.
2012, Michele Hanson, What the Grown-ups Were Doing: An Odyssey Through 1950s Suburbia:

With the sanction and connivance of Irmengarde, her lady-mother, the lovers met nightly in the gardens of Stahleck; and, to crown all, during the temporary absence of the pfalzgraf at the court of the emperor, their hands were united[…]
1839, Joseph Snowe, The Rhine, Legends, Traditions, History, from Cologne to Mainz:
The warrior bishops, electors, pfalzgrafs, and knights of the empire, all swore it was no shame not to be a match for Sathanas.
1857, George Meredith, Farina, page 234:
“Let him! Dost think these simple Englishmen can ever compete with us on the high seas? Pfaff! They are like the silly sheep they raise and are only fit for shearing. […]”
1937, Elinor Whitney Field, “The Coffer Keys” (chapter 5), in Tod of the Fens, The Macmillan Company, page 63:

No, on a foreign journey, the real damage is done pfaffing about in airport lounges, counting down the torture to departure, sitting on the runway, enduring protracted periods of sub-pedestrian taxiing [...].
2001, John McCabe, Snakeskin, Doubleday, →ISBN, page 61:
By my own admission I pfaffed around a bit here but I'm going to claim that I was merely enjoying the moment!
2004, Chris Ward, The controversial Sämisch King's Indian, page 81:

Mr Hicks wrote on his website: "At dusk the rudder cable broke
At dusk the rudder cable broke. "Six hours pfaffing about in the dark and heaving sea saw a fairly unsatisfactory makeshift steering system into place"
2005 September 25, “Atlantic slow row coming to end”, in BBC News:
Pfaugh! — the history of the day was done; but up-stairs, in my naked, noisy room, began a history of the night, which was much more frightful to me.
1892, Thomas Carlyle, “Excursion (Futile Enough) to Paris”, in The Last Words of Thomas Carlyle, Appleton & Co., page 228:
"They live in New York, and he had the effrontery to give me a dinner and ask all his collaborators to it, fat, paunchy men who smelled of money. Pfaugh!"
1976, Robert Herrick, Waste, Ayer Publishing, page 55:
"But not so many as of us, eh? Why do you suppose that is? Because they bob up and down while they pray? Because every Friday they air their bedding out? Pfaugh."
2007, Michael Flynn, Eifelheim, Macmillan, page 167:
